meta.blurb: Nina Alvarez comes to Marlow Bay to sell her late grandmother's café. Instead she finds twelve secret letters that must be delivered, a town full of unsaid words and Eli, the postman she once left behind.
meta.bible: Nina Alvarez: thirty-one, a graphic designer from the city, tired and guarded; she left Marlow Bay at eighteen and never wrote back to Eli. Lucia Alvarez: Nina's grandmother, called Gran, who ran the Love Letter Cafe for forty years and died last month. Eli Marsh: thirty-one, the Marlow Bay postman, kind, steady, Nina's best friend in the summers of their teens; he stayed. Tilly Ward: nineteen, the cheerful waitress who has kept the cafe open. Mr Abel Gold: eighty-three, a regular who writes a letter to his brother Max Gold, from whom he has been apart thirty years after a quarrel about a boat. Max Gold: Abel's brother, a retired boatbuilder in the harbour town of Port Perran. Mrs Fenn: a customer whose letter thanks her old teacher Mr Ash. Tobias: a shy fisherman who writes to Clara, the librarian. Sam: a ten-year-old boy who writes to his father, Mr Dunne, a lifeboat man. Mr Dunmore: a property developer who wants the building for a modern coffee bar. Marlow Bay: the small seaside town. The Love Letter Cafe: the cafe with a blue door, a brass bell and the Letter Wall. The Letter Wall: forty small wooden drawers with brass numbers; customers write what they cannot say and leave it. Gran's rule: a letter is kept for a year and a day and then, if nobody takes it back, Gran quietly posts it. The Ledger: Gran's blue book of names, dates and ticks, with notes such as Reply came. Drawer forty: Nina's, with two envelopes inside. Lighthouse Rock: where Nina and Eli climbed one summer. The Post Office: Eli's workplace on Harbour Street. Voice and tone: warm, quiet and a little funny, a gentle small-town love story about the things people cannot say; the letters help others and finally Nina and Eli; no cruelty; a real ending with a kiss, a staying and a letter. Cafe, Letter, Letters, Drawer, Drawers, Envelope, Postbox, Stamp, Postman, Lifeboat, Lighthouse, Harbour, Ledger, Cinnamon, Espresso, Jar, Roof, Freelance, Contract, Cliff.

B1B2: Nina Alvarez steps off the bus in Marlow Bay with her suitcase and a wet coat. Her grandmother has died, and Nina has come to sell the old café.
The sign over the blue door says The Love Letter Café. Inside, it smells of cinnamon and coffee, and one whole wall is covered with forty small wooden drawers with brass numbers.
Tilly Ward is nineteen, and she has kept the café open since Gran died. She hugs Nina, pushes a hot chocolate into her hands and tells her that the customers still come every morning.
Tilly points to the card above the drawers, written in Gran's hand. It says, Write what you cannot say, and we will keep it safe, and every drawer holds a letter that someone could not send.
Mr Gold, a very old customer, comes in for his tea and sits in the corner to write. He puts the letter in drawer seven and says that he is not ready to send it yet.
That night Nina finds a blue book under the counter. It is full of names, dates and small ticks, and some lines have a note beside them that says Posted.
Slowly Nina begins to understand what the ledger means. After a year and a day, Gran had posted the letters that nobody took back, and many people had received an answer.
Under the counter Nina finds a tin with twelve letters inside. A note says, Nina, please post these, the year and a day is up, I ran out of time, Gran.
Mr Dunmore is a property man in a smart grey coat. He wants to turn the café into a modern coffee bar, and he offers a great deal of money if Nina signs within four weeks.
Nina's boss in the city calls and says he needs her back in a month. She says yes, and then she looks at the tin and decides to deliver the twelve letters first, as one last favour to Gran.
Nina does not know the town any more, so she goes to the post office for help. The postman who looks up from the sorting table is tall, tired and smiling, and his name is Eli Marsh.

Years ago, Nina and Eli were best friends every summer, and they climbed rocks and ate chips on the harbour wall. When Nina went away to study, she stopped answering his letters, and she has never explained why.
Eli looks at the envelopes and smiles sadly at the handwriting. Letters in that hand have passed through his bag for years, he says, so he agrees to help her find every address.
The first letter was written by Mrs Fenn to her old teacher, Mr Ash. He reads it in his garden and tells Nina and Eli that nobody has ever thanked him in his whole life.
The very next morning a reply arrives at the café for Mrs Fenn. Tilly cheers, and Nina feels a small warm glow that she has not felt in years.
The second letter is from a shy fisherman named Tobias to Clara, the librarian. Nina worries that it is too private, but Eli reminds her that Gran trusted the people who wrote.
Clara reads the letter at her desk and turns pink. That evening she walks to the harbour and sits beside Tobias on a bench, while Nina and Eli watch from far away.
On the way home, they walk along the cliff path. They laugh about the summer they climbed Lighthouse Rock, and the old ease between them begins to return.
The third letter is from Sam, who is ten, to his father at the lifeboat station. Mr Dunne reads it between emergencies, and then he picks Sam up and hugs him for a long time.
Word spreads through Marlow Bay that the letters are really being delivered. Soon there is a line out of the door, and Tilly cannot make the coffee fast enough.
Nina ties on an apron and learns the coffee machine. She burns herself twice and spills a pot of milk, but she finds, to her surprise, that she is smiling.
Mr Gold has not come in for three days, and Tilly is worried. Nina visits his small flat and finds him in bed with a bad cough, and he gives her the letter from drawer seven.
The letter is for Max Gold, his brother, whom he has not spoken to for thirty years because of a quarrel about a boat. Nina promises to break Gran's rule and post it now.
Eli finds the address in Port Perran and borrows his cousin's car. Mr Gold insists on coming too, and he sits in the back in a blanket, saying nothing for the whole journey.
A man opens the door of a small house by the harbour. He looks at Mr Gold for a long time and says, You are late, and then the two old brothers fall into each other's arms.
Back at the café that night, Nina and Eli stand very close at the door. Just as he leans toward her, a customer pushes the door open, the bell rings, and they jump apart.
In the days that follow, Nina and Eli deliver the other nine letters in the rain and the sun. There is a thank-you to a nurse, a sorry to a neighbour and a letter for a grandson abroad.
Nina's boss calls from the city and says that he needs her back soon. He tells her that she must be at her desk on Monday week, and before she can think, she says yes.
Mr Dunmore returns with the contract and a gold pen. Nina says that she will sign on Friday week, after the last of the letters, and Tilly hears and has to turn away.
Later Tilly says that Eli visited Gran every Sunday for a year. Gran had asked him not to tell Nina how ill she was, because she did not want to call her home out of pity.
Nina marches into the post office and tells Eli that he should have told her about Gran. He says that he made a promise, and that Gran was proud of her and did not want to bring her home out of pity.
Nina says that Eli stayed in Marlow Bay because he was too afraid to leave. Eli answers that she left because she was too afraid to stay, and neither of them can take it back.
That night, the café is empty and the rain beats on the windows. Nina reads her emails from the city and feels that she has been running away her whole life.
Gran's note had said that drawer forty was Nina's alone. Nina finds the key in the tin, and inside the drawer are two envelopes, one in Gran's writing and one in a boy's hand.
Nina opens Eli's letter and reads it slowly, with tears in her eyes. He wrote it at eighteen, and he does not ask her to stay, only to remember that a door with a bell will open.
Tilly arrives early with the milk and finds Nina still reading. She says that Eli asked Gran to keep the letter until Nina came home, and Gran kept it safe for thirteen years.
At last Nina understands why she never wrote back to Eli. She was afraid that if she wrote, she would come home and never be able to get away again.
Nina takes a clean sheet of café paper and starts to write. She writes one draft, then another, and finally a short one that says exactly what she means.
At dawn Nina hurries to the post office, where Eli is sorting the first mail. She says sorry and holds out her letter, and he reads it standing up.
Eli puts the letter down on the counter and takes her hands. He kisses her among the sacks of mail, and outside the window Tilly cheers and a seagull flies away in alarm.
Mr Dunmore arrives to collect the signed contract, and Nina says no. He warns her that the roof leaks and that Gran left debts, so the café may close within a year.
Tilly and Eli have an idea that they have not yet told Nina. They will hold a Letter Night, when the whole town comes to write letters and puts a coin in a jar to mend the roof.
They put up posters all over town, and Tilly paints a sign for the window. Eli arranges for the post office to collect from a real postbox at the café, every Friday.
On Letter Night the café is packed to the walls with people writing. Mrs Fenn and Mr Ash, Tobias and Clara, Sam and his father and Mr Gold with his brother Max are all there.
By midnight the jar is full of coins, and Tilly counts them twice. Max Gold, who used to build boats, stands up and says that he will mend the roof for nothing.
Mr Dunmore watches from the back of the room with his gold pen. He reads the card above the drawers, puts the pen away, and slips out of the door without making an offer.
On Monday morning Nina calls her boss in the city. She says that she is leaving her job, but that she would like to work for him as a freelance designer from Marlow Bay.
That night, Nina opens Gran's envelope with Eli beside her. Gran writes that the café was never the point, and that the point is to be brave enough to say what matters.
Eli fixes a forty-first drawer to the wall, and Nina writes her first letter for it. She does not tell anyone what it says, and she locks it and puts the key around her neck.

A year and a day later, Nina opens drawer forty-one, takes out her letter and walks to the post office. She hands it to Eli, who reads the three words inside, and then he comes around the counter to kiss her.
C1C2: The bus left Nina Alvarez at the foot of Harbour Street with a suitcase, a wet coat and a heaviness she could not name. She had not seen Marlow Bay in thirteen years, and now she had come back only because her grandmother had died and left her a small café she had no intention of keeping. The gulls, the rain and the smell of salt greeted her as though she had never been away.

Over the blue door a faded sign read The Love Letter Café, and when Nina pushed it open, a brass bell rang exactly as it had when she was a child. The air inside was warm and thick with cinnamon and coffee, and along the far wall stood forty small wooden drawers, each with a brass number and a tiny lock. She had forgotten how much the place had always looked like a secret waiting to be opened.

A girl of nineteen with a pencil stuck in her hair came out from behind the counter and hugged Nina before she could say a word. This was Tilly Ward, who had worked for Gran after school for two years and had kept the café open every single day since the funeral. She pressed a hot chocolate into Nina's cold hands and said, a little shyly, that the customers kept coming and nobody knew what else to do.

Tilly pointed to a card above the drawers, written in Gran's looping hand, which read, Write what you cannot say, and we will keep it safe. People came in, she explained, wrote a letter to someone they could not face, and left it in a numbered drawer, and Gran kept it there for a year and a day. Most of the customers, she added with a shrug, never came back to ask for their letters.

At ten o'clock an old man in a tweed cap shuffled in, ordered a pot of tea and spent half an hour writing with great care in the corner. When he had finished, he walked to the wall and slid his envelope into drawer seven, turned the little key and put it in his pocket. Mr Gold, Tilly whispered, had been writing the same letter for years, and he was never quite ready to send it.

That night, after Tilly had gone home, Nina found a blue ledger tucked under the counter and sat down with it beneath the small lamp. Every page was ruled in Gran's neat columns of names, dates and drawer numbers, and beside many of the entries was a small tick and one word, Posted. A few of them had a second note in the margin that said, in green ink, Reply came.

Slowly the truth came clear: when a year and a day had passed and nobody had returned for a letter, her grandmother had quietly posted it herself. She had been giving people the courage they lacked, one envelope at a time, and half of Marlow Bay had been receiving answers from people they thought had forgotten them. The town had a name for it, Nina would learn later, though nobody had ever spoken it aloud: Lucia's post.

At the very bottom of the cupboard, behind the sugar, Nina found a battered biscuit tin that rattled with envelopes. Inside lay twelve letters, each with a name on the front, and on top of them a note in her grandmother's hand that read, Nina, please post these, their year is up and I ran out of time, love, Gran. Nina sat down on the floor with the tin in her lap and did not move for a long while.

The next morning a man in a smart grey coat strolled in, looked at the drawers as though they were an unusual stain and introduced himself as Mr Dunmore. He wished to turn the café into a sleek modern coffee bar, he said, and he was prepared to pay a handsome sum if Nina would sign the papers within four weeks. It was more money than she had ever imagined owning, and it made her feel strangely ill.

That afternoon her boss telephoned from the city to say, kindly but firmly, that she was needed back at her desk in a month. She agreed, hung up and looked at the biscuit tin in front of her, and a decision formed that she could not have explained to anyone. She would sell the café, but first she would deliver all twelve letters, because it was the last thing her grandmother had asked of her.

Since she no longer knew who lived where in Marlow Bay, Nina walked to the post office on Harbour Street to ask for help. The man at the sorting table looked up from a heap of parcels, and she felt the floor shift beneath her, because it was Eli Marsh, taller and broader than she remembered, in a blue postman's jacket. He set down the parcel he was holding and said her name as though he had been saying it for years.

Thirteen years earlier, Nina and Eli had spent every summer together, climbing the cliffs, sharing chips on the harbour wall and promising that nothing would ever change. Then she had left for university at eighteen, and Eli's letters had gone unanswered, one after another, until he had stopped writing. She had never explained why, and standing in front of him now, she realised that she still had no good answer.

Eli took the envelopes from her one by one and ran his thumb along the looping handwriting with a sad, fond smile. Letters in that same hand, he admitted, had passed through his bag for years, and he had long suspected where they came from, though he had never asked. He knew every door in Marlow Bay, he told her, and if Nina wanted to deliver twelve letters in four weeks, he would be glad to show her the way.

The first letter had been written by Mrs Fenn, now a grandmother herself, to Mr Ash, the teacher who had once convinced her that she could read. They found him in his garden among the beans, and he read it standing up, his lips moving and his hands trembling slightly. Nobody in forty years of teaching had ever thanked him, he told them, and he blew his nose with great energy and invited them in for tea.

The very next morning a cream envelope arrived at the café, addressed in shaky capitals to Mrs Fenn, care of the Love Letter Café. Tilly whooped and waved it like a flag, and Nina, who had spent years in an office where nothing ever came back, felt a small warm glow spread through her chest. It was the first time she had understood what her grandmother had been doing all those years.

The second letter was from Tobias, a shy fisherman with enormous hands, and it was addressed to Clara, the librarian, in a hand that shook even on paper. Nina stood outside the library door, convinced that it was too private to deliver, until Eli reminded her gently that her grandmother had always trusted the people who wrote. They agreed that Nina would hand it over herself and then slip quietly away.

Clara read the letter twice at her desk, turned the colour of a rose and then, to Nina's amazement, put on her coat in the middle of the working day. That evening Nina and Eli watched from the end of the harbour wall as the librarian walked slowly toward a fisherman mending nets, and sat down beside him. Neither of them could hear what was said, but nobody on that bench was in a hurry to leave.

On the way home they took the cliff path, with the tide thundering below and the lighthouse standing white against the clouds. They laughed about the summer they had climbed Lighthouse Rock at sixteen, when Eli had been too frightened to come down and Nina had talked him off it for an hour. It was astonishing how easily the old friendship slipped back, like a hand into a worn glove.

The third letter had been written by Sam, a ten-year-old boy, to his father, a lifeboat man who was so often at sea that the boy sometimes forgot what his face looked like. Nina and Eli delivered it at the station between two emergency calls, and Mr Dunne read it standing in the doorway with his oilskin dripping. Then he lifted his son off the ground and held him for so long that the kettle boiled dry.

News travels fast in a small town, and by the end of the week everyone in Marlow Bay knew that Lucia's letters were being delivered again. People who had not entered the café in years queued out of the door, clutching pens and nervous expressions, and Tilly battled alone with the old coffee machine. It sighed, spluttered and hissed at her, and the cinnamon rolls vanished by ten.

Tilly was drowning, so Nina tied on an apron and learned the temperamental coffee machine within the hour, scalding her thumb twice and flooding the counter with milk. Customers laughed with her rather than at her, an old fisherman gave her a tip, and by closing time she realised that she had smiled more in a single day than in the whole previous year. It frightened her slightly, because it felt so very much like belonging somewhere at last.

When Mr Gold failed to appear for three mornings in a row, Tilly grew anxious, so Nina carried a pot of soup to his small flat above the chandler's. She found him in bed with a bad cough and a tartan blanket, looking smaller than she remembered, and he pressed the key of drawer seven into her hand. Would she fetch his letter, he asked, because he had a feeling that a year and a day might be too long to wait.

The letter was addressed to Max Gold, Mr Gold's younger brother, whom he had not spoken to in thirty years because of a foolish quarrel over the ownership of a boat. His pride had grown over the years like a wall, he told Nina quietly, and now that he was old he could not remember what had been so important. She promised that she would break her grandmother's rule and deliver it at once.

Eli tracked down Max Gold's address in the harbour town of Port Perran, borrowed his cousin's small blue car and drove them down the coast road on a bright cold Saturday. Mr Gold had insisted on coming, in spite of his cough, and he sat in the back under a blanket, staring out at the sea and saying nothing at all. Nina watched his reflection in the window and saw how tightly he held his own hands.

A white-haired man opened the door of a small house beside the harbour, and for a long moment the two brothers simply looked at each other, with the same nose, the same stubborn chin and thirty years between them. Max said, in a gruff voice, that Abel was late, and Abel said that he knew, and then they were in each other's arms, shaking. Nina held the unopened letter in her hand and found that she did not need to give it to anyone.

That night, back at the café, Nina and Eli stood in the doorway in the soft light of the street lamp, so close that she could feel his breath. He leaned toward her slowly, as if asking a question, and the brass bell above their heads suddenly jangled as Tilly hurried in to collect her forgotten umbrella. They sprang apart, and Tilly, who understood far more than she pretended, found the umbrella with exaggerated difficulty.

Over the next few days they delivered the remaining nine letters in sunshine and showers, a thank-you to a night nurse, an apology to a neighbour and a proud word for a grandson abroad. Nina learned every lane and shortcut in Marlow Bay, and she began to see the town not as the place she had run from, but as a thousand quiet stories waiting for someone to open the right door. Eli carried the umbrella and, whenever he thought she was not looking, watched her.

While the café bustled around her, Nina's boss telephoned from the city to say that her leave was over and that she must be back at her desk on Monday week. She heard herself say yes, in the cheerful and efficient voice she had used for years, and then she stood with the phone in her hand feeling slightly sick. The wall of drawers seemed to look at her, patiently, as though it were waiting for the rest of her answer.

Mr Dunmore returned the next day with a thick contract and a gold pen, smiling like a man who already owned the building. Nina told him, without quite meeting his eyes, that she would sign on Friday week, once the last of the letters had been delivered. Behind the counter Tilly had heard every word, and she turned away quickly so that no one would see her face.

Later, wiping the same table over and over, Tilly told Nina something that made her go cold. Eli had visited her grandmother every Sunday for the whole of the last year, she said, and Gran had made him promise not to tell Nina how ill she was. She had not wanted her granddaughter to come home out of pity, Tilly explained, and the promise had been breaking Eli's heart ever since.

Nina marched into the post office with her cheeks burning and told Eli, in front of three customers and a parrot in a cage, that he should have told her. He answered quietly that he had made a promise to a dying woman, who had been so proud of her granddaughter's career and had not wanted her to come home out of pity. His voice cracked on the last word, but Nina was too hurt to hear it.

In her anger Nina said that Eli had stayed in Marlow Bay all his life only because he was too afraid to leave it, and the words landed like stones. He looked at her for a long moment, very pale, and answered that perhaps that was true, but that she had left because she was afraid of exactly the same thing, and that she had been running ever since. She walked out, and the post office bell jangled behind her like a slammed door.

That night the café stood empty and silent, with the rain drumming steadily on the glass and the forty drawers glinting in the lamplight. Nina scrolled through her emails from the city, a hundred of them, each one demanding something, and she realised with a slow chill that she had been running from one task to another for thirteen years. Eli had been right about her, and that was exactly why it hurt so much.

Her grandmother's note had said that drawer forty belonged to Nina alone, and at last she fetched the little key from the bottom of the tin. Inside lay two envelopes, the first marked in Gran's looping hand, For Nina, to be read last, and the second addressed in careful, boyish handwriting, Nina Alvarez, for when she comes home. She knew whose it was before she touched it, and her fingers began to shake.

The letter was dated the summer she left, and it was written in a young man's careful handwriting that she would have known anywhere. He was not asking her to stay, Eli had written, because he wanted her to go and become everything she could be. He only wanted her to remember that there was a blue door in Marlow Bay with a bell that would always ring for her, and that if she never wrote he would understand, but if she did, he would answer.

Tilly arrived early with the milk and found Nina on the floor beside the open drawer, still holding the letter, with her eyes red from crying. Eli had asked Gran to keep it safe until Nina came home, she explained gently, and Gran had refused to post it for thirteen years because he had asked her to wait. It was the only letter in the whole café that had broken its year and a day, and it had never been posted at all.

As the sun climbed over the harbour, Nina understood at last why she had never answered Eli's letters, and the truth was so simple that it was almost funny. She had been afraid that a single reply would pull her back to Marlow Bay forever, and that she would never become anything if she came home. It had not occurred to her that she might do both, and that a door that rings for you need not be a cage.

Nina took a clean sheet from the pile beside the drawers and began to write, and the first draft was too long, the second too proud and the third too frightened. By the time the milk had arrived, the floor was ankle-deep in crumpled paper, and the fourth attempt was only a few short lines long. They said exactly what she meant, which was the only thing a letter was ever really for.

At dawn Nina hurried down Harbour Street to the post office, where Eli was sorting the first sack of mail in the pale light. She said that she was sorry, then said it again, and held out the folded letter without another word, and he read it standing very still while the clock ticked behind him. It began, Dear Eli, I am writing back, and I am sorry it took thirteen years, and he had to read it twice because his eyes kept blurring.

Eli put the letter down very carefully on the counter, as though it were made of glass, then crossed the room and took both of her hands. He kissed her among the sacks and parcels, gently at first and then with thirteen years of waiting, while the sorting machine clattered on unnoticed. Outside the window, Tilly, who had followed her to see what would happen, punched the air and startled a seagull from the roof.

On Friday morning Mr Dunmore swept in to collect his signature, and Nina told him, quietly and firmly, that the café was not for sale. He sighed, tapped his gold pen on the folder and reminded her that the roof leaked, that her grandmother had left debts and that without his money the café would close within a year. He was right about the roof, Nina knew, and she lay awake that night with the problem pressing down on her chest.

It was Tilly who thought of it first, and Eli who added the details, and they presented the plan to Nina over the counter with a hand-drawn poster. They would hold a Letter Night at the café, to which the whole of Marlow Bay would come to write the letters they had been putting off. Each guest would put a coin in a jar to help mend the roof, and Nina was not at all sure it would work, but she found that she very much wanted it to.

For the next week the three of them filled Marlow Bay with posters, and Tilly painted a sign across the café window in letters as tall as a child. Eli, using a little quiet persuasion at the sorting office, arranged for the brass postbox by the door to become an official one, emptied every Friday afternoon. From now on a letter written in the café could travel anywhere in the world, without anyone needing to be brave in secret.

On Letter Night the café was packed to the walls, and candles flickered on every table while pens scratched in a hushed, happy murmur. Mrs Fenn sat beside Mr Ash, Tobias held hands with Clara at the corner table, Sam perched on his father's knee, and Mr Gold, much recovered, sat with his brother Max, arguing cheerfully over the sugar. Nina looked around at all of them and understood that her grandmother's letters had built a town.

By midnight the great glass jar was overflowing with coins and folded notes, and Tilly counted them twice and shouted the total across the room. Max Gold, who had spent his life building wooden boats and knew a thing or two about keeping out the weather, rose slowly to his feet and announced that he would mend the roof for nothing. His brother, beside him, blew his nose so loudly that the whole room burst into applause.

At the back of the room, by the door, Mr Dunmore stood watching with his gold pen in his pocket and an unreadable look on his face. He read the old card above the drawers twice, Write what you cannot say, and we will keep it safe, and something in his expression slowly changed. Then he put his hat on and slipped out into the night without making an offer, and Nina never saw his gold pen again.

On Monday morning Nina telephoned her boss in the city, and for the first time in years she did not apologise before she spoke. She told him she was leaving her post, but that she would happily design for his company as a freelancer from a small café by the sea, if he would have her. He was silent for a moment and then said, with unexpected kindness, that he would be glad to, and that he had been wondering when she would ask.

That night, after the last customer had gone, Nina sat on the old sofa with Eli's arm around her and opened her grandmother's letter at last. The café had never been the point, Gran had written, and neither had the drawers or the stamps, because people were simply braver on paper than they were out loud. Stay or go, my darling, she had finished, but whatever you do, write to the people who matter, and write soon.

Eli carried in a new wooden drawer with a gleaming brass number, forty-one, and screwed it to the wall beside the others with a great deal of care. Nina wrote a letter that she did not show to anyone, folded it into an envelope, slid it into the drawer and turned the little key. She hung the key around her neck, where it sat close to her heart, and it felt like the beginning of something rather than the end.

A year and a day later, Nina unlocked drawer forty-one, took out her letter and walked down Harbour Street in the spring sunshine to the post office. She handed it across the counter to Eli, who opened it with care and read the three words inside, which were, I am home. He came around the counter without a single word, kissed her in front of the whole queue, and the bell above the door rang as if it had been waiting for this all along.
